interactionPlan.concept: A corner acts as a natural camera because its edge progressively blocks light, meaning the hidden scene's 1D image can be reconstructed by taking the spatial derivative of the observed intensity on the ground.
learningObjectives: Understand how an occluding edge (corner) integrates light from a hidden scene.
Explain why the observed signal on the ground is the cumulative sum of the angular light distribution of the hidden scene.
Demonstrate how to reconstruct the hidden scene's light profile using the spatial derivative (differences) of the observed intensity.
interactionPlan.keyInsight: The shadow cast by a corner acts as a computational lens: because the edge creates a step-like occlusion, the difference in light between two adjacent spots on the floor is exactly the light coming from a single, specific angle in the hidden scene.

interactions.label: Hidden Scene
interactions.effect: Changes the hidden world light distribution (lw) between 'Book Example', 'Single Spotlight', and 'Two Distinct Sources', updating both plots instantly.
interactions.teaches: How different light distributions in the hidden world project into distinct cumulative shadow profiles on the floor.

interactions.label: Floor Position (n)
interactions.effect: Highlights the specific index n on both plots and visualizes which light rays from the hidden world (indices >= n) are reaching this spot on the floor.
interactions.teaches: The geometric relation of the corner camera: a sensor at position n only receives light from angles greater than or equal to n, while smaller angles are blocked.

demo_steps.title: The Hidden and Observed Signals
demo_steps.narration: Look at the two plots. The left plot, lw, represents the light intensity coming from different angles in a hidden room. The right plot, ls, is the actual light intensity measured along the floor near a corner. Notice how the floor intensity gradually decreases as we move from left (n = 0) to right (n = 12).
demo_steps.focus: The overall shape comparison between the two discrete stem plots.

demo_steps.title: Understanding the Occlusion
demo_steps.narration: Drag the 'Floor Position' slider to n = 5. At this position, the corner blocks all light rays from angles 0 through 4. Therefore, the measured intensity ls(5) is the sum of only the remaining unblocked light sources (from 5 to 12), which equals 10.
demo_steps.focus: The summation of lw values from index 5 to 12 resulting in the value of ls at n = 5.

demo_steps.title: The Secret is the Derivative
demo_steps.narration: Move the slider from n = 8 to n = 9. Notice how ls drops from 10 to 9. This drop of exactly 1 unit corresponds to the light source lw(8) = 1 being blocked. Because each step blocks exactly one angular channel, subtracting adjacent values on the floor (ls(n) - ls(n+1)) perfectly reconstructs the hidden scene lw(n)!
demo_steps.focus: The step-by-step difference between adjacent stems on the right plot yielding the height of the stem on the left plot.

demo_steps.title: Spotting a Single Light Source
demo_steps.narration: Switch the 'Hidden Scene' to 'Single Spotlight'. Notice that a single localized source in the hidden world (lw) creates a sharp, step-like shadow edge on the floor (ls). Taking the derivative of this step edge localizes the spotlight perfectly.
demo_steps.focus: The mapping of a single peak in lw to a step function in ls, emphasizing the integration/differentiation duality.

interactionPlan.reconstructionNotes: The visualization should display two side-by-side discrete stem plots matching the style of the original figure. The left plot is labeled lw (world light) and the right plot is labeled ls (sensor light). Both have x-axes labeled 'n' ranging from 0 to 12. Points are represented by blue dots with vertical lines extending down to the axis. When active, an interactive light ray geometry diagram (a 2D schematic of a corner blocking rays) can be displayed above or alongside the plots to clarify the line-of-sight mapping.
